segments.title: Cutty Sark's rigging shows a clipper's complexity
segments.summary: Cutty Sark's surviving rigging gives a quick visual measure of a sailing clipper's complexity before the visit turns to the cargo trade that rewarded speed.
segments.body: The visit opens on Cutty Sark's rigging. The dense arrangement of lines gives a quick sense of the equipment carried by a fast sailing ship. Seeing the rig in place makes its complexity much clearer than a short description could. The camera then moves from the ship's structure to the cargo trade that rewarded speed.

evidence.note: Aboard Cutty Sark, Dr. Clarke directs attention to the visible rigging and says it reveals how remarkable these ships were.

segments.title: Tea chests and standardised cargo
segments.summary: Tea chests provide a short comparison between early standardised cargo packaging, wrapped wool, and modern intermodal containers, then link uniform loads to the speed of the tea clippers.
segments.body: Tea chests are presented as an early form of standardised transport packaging and a precursor to the logic of modern intermodal containers. Their repeatable box shape contrasts with wool, which was standardised through wrapping. Uniform packages made goods easier to organise and move at large scale, while tea clippers competed through speed. The comparison links Cutty Sark's design purpose to the commercial system around her. It is a brief analogy about transport standardisation rather than a history of modern containerisation.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke identifies tea chests as an early standardized transport box and contrasts them with modern intermodal containers and wrapped wool.
He links mass-scale standardized goods transport to the speed-focused role of tea clippers.
